6555.stem:
The flow of water through a series of pipes is shown in the network below. The water flows from the source ($S$) to the sink ($T$) and the numbers on the edges show the maximum capacity of each pipe in litres per minute.

\exfigure{819_q37_1}

figures.cap: blank flow network to label flows

parts.latex: Find the maximum flow from $S$ to $T$.

On the diagram below, label the flows along each edge that would be required to achieve the maximum flow.

\exfigure{819_q37_2}
By increasing the capacity of one edge in the network, the maximum flow could be increased by 3 litres per minute. Identify the edge that could be increased.

solutions.latex:
By the maximum-flow minimum-cut theorem, the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.

Cut the network between $\{S,A,C,D,E\}$ and $\{B,T\}$. The edges crossing from the first set to the second are $AB$, $CB$ and $ET$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{cut} &= 10+6+18 \\ &= 34 \end{aligned}$$
A flow of 34 is achievable (see part (b)), so no smaller cut exists.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum flow} = 34 \text{ litres per minute}$$
criteria: Finds a cut or a flow, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: networkx max flow = 34, min cut AB+CB+ET.

solutions.latex:
One set of flows that gives 34 L/min:
$$\begin{aligned} SA&=16, & SC&=9, & SD&=9, \\ AB&=10, & AC&=6, & CB&=6, \\ CE&=9, & DE&=9, & BT&=16, \\ ET&=18 \end{aligned}$$
Check conservation at each vertex: at $A$, $16=10+6$; at $C$, $9+6=6+9$; at $D$, $9=9$; at $B$, $10+6=16$; at $E$, $9+9=18$. Flow out of $S$ is $16+9+9=34$.

\exfigure{819_q37_s1}

meta.self_check: Conservation verified at every vertex, no edge exceeds capacity.
meta.generated_note: The maximum flow can be distributed in more than one way; other valid distributions with total 34 should be accepted.

solutions.latex:
The maximum flow can only increase if an edge of the minimum cut is enlarged. The minimum cut consists of $AB$, $CB$ and $ET$.

Increasing $ET$ by 3 only raises the flow by 2, because another cut then limits the flow. Increasing $AB$ by 3 (to 13) or $CB$ by 3 (to 9) raises the maximum flow from 34 to 37, the capacity of the cut at $BT$ and $ET$ ($19+18$).
$$\therefore\ \text{increase edge } AB \text{ (or edge } CB\text{)}$$

meta.self_check: Tested each edge +3 in max flow: AB and CB both give 37; ET gives 36.
meta.generated_note: Both AB and CB give an increase of 3; either should be accepted.

6670.stem:
The network diagram shows a series of water pipes and sprinklers in a section of an underground lawn watering system. The vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ and $F$ represent the sprinklers. The edges represent the underground water pipes which connect the sprinklers. The numbers on the edges represent the maximum capacity (in litres per hour) of the water pipes.

\exfigure{825_q35_1}

figures.cap: flow network with an invalid cut drawn as a dashed curve

parts.latex:
In the diagram below, an invalid cut has been marked on the network. Explain why it is invalid.

\exfigure{825_q35_2}
Determine the maximum flow of the network.

solutions.latex:
A valid cut must separate the source $A$ from the sink $F$, so that every path from $A$ to $F$ is cut. In the diagram, both $A$ and $F$ lie on the same side (below) of the dashed line.

$$\therefore\ \text{the cut is invalid because it does not separate the source from the sink}$$

meta.self_check: Looked at the cut position relative to the source and sink arrows in the figure: both lie below the dashed curve.
meta.generated_note: The cut also crosses edge BD twice, which is another way to see it is not a valid cut.

solutions.latex:
By the maximum flow, minimum cut theorem, the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.

Consider the cut separating $\{A, B, C, D\}$ from $\{E, F\}$. It cuts the edges directed from the source side to the sink side: $D\to F$ and $C\to E$. The edge $E\to D$ points back to the source side, so it is not counted.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{capacity} &= 180+95 \\ &= 275 \text{ litres per hour} \end{aligned}$$
This flow can be achieved: send $135$ along $A\to B\to D$, $140$ along $A\to C$ (of which $95$ goes $C\to E\to F$ and $45$ goes $C\to D$), and $D\to F$ carries $135+45=180$. Total into $F$ is $180+95=275$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum flow is } 275 \text{ litres per hour}$$
criteria: Finds a valid cut or a flow of a smaller value, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: Direction of arrows read from the figure; flow of 275 verified against all edge capacities and matches the cut.
meta.generated_note: The arrow on DE was read as pointing from E to D.

825_q35_1.notes: Flow network with vertices A–F placed as measured, mid-edge direction arrows as filled Latex heads (rule 4), 0.6pt lines, capacities and italic vertex names at the crop's positions (rules 3, 19).

825_q35_2.notes: Same network as 825_q35_1 plus the invalid cut, a smooth curve fitted to the crop's dashed line and drawn in the house aux dash (rule 3, short fine dashes instead of the scan's long dashes). Rule 11: '135' moved just below the cut (the crop had the cut running through it) and '80' lifted slightly clear of the cut. Look at F: it sits just under the cut as in the crop and may be very close to the dashes.

6754.stem:
A museum is planning an exhibition using five rooms. The vertices $A,B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ represent the five rooms. The numbers on the edges represent The maximum number of people per hour who can pass through the security checkpoints between the rooms.

\exfigure{827_q38_1}

figures.cap: flow network Entry-A-B-C-D-E-Exit with a dotted cut

parts.latex: What is the capacity of the cut shown?
What is the flow capacity of the network?

solutions.latex:
Add the capacities of the edges crossing the cut:
$$\begin{aligned} 130+90+70 &= 290 \end{aligned}$$

By the max-flow min-cut theorem, the flow capacity is the minimum cut.
$$\therefore\ 230$$

The original score of 0.833 is just under target: what is left is the dotted cut drawn as fine dashes, plus small label offsets.

6799.stem:
The network diagram shows the maximum flow of traffic, in vehicles per hour, between along several streets in a congested town.

\exfigure{828_q40_1}

parts.latex: It is known that the minimum cut of this network cuts through edge DF. The maximum flow of the network is 530 vehicle per hour. Determine the value of $x$.

A new road from D to G is being built. The flow capacity of this road is 30 vehicles per hour. Will this road increase the maximum flow of the entire network to 560 vehicles per hour? Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
The minimum cut passes through $DF$, so the maximum flow equals the sum of the capacities cut.
$$x + 150 + 250 = 530$$
$$x = 530 - 400$$
$$\therefore\ x = 130$$
criteria: Sets up an equation but does not use the correct minimum cut, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: No. The capacity out of the source along $s \to A$ is still $550$ vehicles per hour, so the maximum flow cannot exceed $550$, and so cannot reach $560$.

meta.format_note: Source says 'from s to A'; kept as $s \to A$ edge label.

parts.latex:
To reduce congestion at Tao National Park, one-way trails are used to direct visitors from the Visitors Centre to the Lookout. The network flow diagram below shows the layout of trails.

\exfigure{2846_q7a_1}

The trails pass through picnic areas which are labelled R through to X.

The capacity of each trail, in visitors per hour, is shown beside the trial.

All visitors return to the Visitors Centre along a single one-way trail which has a capacity of 160 visitors per hour. (This trail is not shown.)
What is the maximum flow of visitors from the Visitors Centre to the Lookout?
What increase to the capacity of a single trail would allow the return trail to operate at its full capacity of 160?

criteria: Correct answer, using the minimum cut
Gives 149, with markings showing a cut, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The cuts below $160$ are $145$, $149$ and $152$. The smallest cut needs an increase of $15$ to reach $160$.

Increasing $TV$, $TW$ or $TX$ by $15$ would raise the $145$ and $149$ cuts to at least $160$. However, this would not affect the $152$ cut.

$$\therefore\ TV \text{ or } TX \text{ increased by } 15$$

meta.source_flag: Source working says TV, TW, TX raise the 145 and 149 cuts but not the 152 cut, then concludes only TV or TX; TW is excluded without explanation.

parts.latex: What is the maximum flow of water through the network of pipes?
Insert the minimum cut on the network diagram.

solutions.latex:
The maximum flow equals the total of the flows along the paths used:

$$\begin{aligned} ABC &= 6 \\ ADC &= 2 \\ ADEC &= 6 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Maximum flow} = 14 \text{ L/min}$$
